DOCUMENT:
Vendor Comparison: Standard Parcel Delivery Contract
Larkspur Home, Operations, June 2026

1. Purpose
Our contract with our current standard-delivery carrier ends on 30 September 2026. This paper compares three shortlisted carriers and recommends which should carry our standard (two-to-four-day) parcels from October.

2. Volumes and requirements
We dispatch an average of 42,000 standard parcels a month: about 70% weigh under 2 kg (cushions, textiles, small homeware) and 30% weigh 2 to 10 kg (lamps, mirrors, small furniture). Our requirements are on-time delivery of at least 95%, a damage rate below 0.5%, full tracking, and a returns service.

Damage and loss matter to us commercially. Each damaged or lost parcel costs us on average £48 in replacement stock, return shipping and customer service time, and damaged items are the most common cause of one-star reviews.

3. Trial
Between 1 April and 31 May 2026, each shortlisted carrier delivered a share of our orders, allocated at random by the warehouse management system, about 5,000 parcels per carrier. We measured on-time delivery against the promised date, damage reported by customers within 14 days, and lost parcels.

Table 1. Prices and trial performance
Carrier | Price, under 2 kg | Price, 2-10 kg | On-time delivery | Damage rate | Lost per 10,000 parcels
SwiftDrop | £3.10 | £4.60 | 96.2% | 0.4% | 3
ParcelLine | £2.85 | £4.95 | 93.1% | 0.9% | 8
Meridian | £3.30 | £4.40 | 97.5% | 0.3% | 2

On-time delivery was above 95% for all three carriers during the trial, and all three offer full tracking and a returns service.

4. Cost comparison
Applying our 70/30 weight mix, the average cost per parcel is £3.55 for SwiftDrop, £3.48 for ParcelLine and £3.63 for Meridian. On 42,000 parcels a month, the monthly cost would be £149,100 for SwiftDrop, £146,160 for ParcelLine and £152,460 for Meridian. ParcelLine is therefore the cheapest option, saving £2,940 a month against SwiftDrop and £6,300 a month against Meridian, or between about £35,000 and £76,000 a year.

5. Customer contact
"Where is my order?" contacts are our largest single category of customer service enquiry. During the trial, ParcelLine deliveries generated 6 such contacts per 1,000 parcels, compared with 11 for SwiftDrop and 10 for Meridian. ParcelLine's live-tracking app clearly reduces customer contacts, and at an average handling cost of £3.20 per contact this would save about £670 a month at our volumes. From 1 May, ParcelLine parcels also carried our new proactive delivery-day text message, which we were testing on one carrier before rolling it out.

6. Other considerations
All three carriers can collect from our warehouse daily at 6 pm. ParcelLine and SwiftDrop offer a 12-month contract; Meridian requires 24 months. SwiftDrop and Meridian have both handled our peak-season volumes for other retailers of similar size, while ParcelLine's references were mainly from fashion retailers with lighter parcels.

All three carriers integrate with our warehouse management system through standard interfaces, and none would require changes to our packing process or labelling. Each offers recipients a delivery-preference service to nominate a safe place or a neighbour, and each provides proof-of-delivery photographs, which our customer service team has found useful in resolving disputes.

7. Recommendation
ParcelLine offers the lowest delivery cost, met our service requirements in the trial and reduces customer contacts through its tracking app. We recommend awarding the standard parcel contract to ParcelLine for 12 months from 1 October 2026, saving up to £76,000 a year against the alternatives.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [misread_evidence] at: "On-time delivery was above 95% for all three carriers during the trial" -- Table 1 shows ParcelLine's on-time delivery was 93.1%, below the 95% requirement. The claim (and the recommendation that ParcelLine 'met our service requirements') misreads the table; ParcelLine's 0.9% damage rate also fails the stated 0.5% requirement.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "ParcelLine's live-tracking app clearly reduces customer contacts" -- The document states that from 1 May ParcelLine parcels alone also carried the new proactive delivery-day text message. That concurrent intervention confounds the comparison, so the lower contact rate cannot be attributed to ParcelLine's tracking app.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "ParcelLine is therefore the cheapest option, saving £2,940 a month against SwiftDrop" -- The cost comparison ignores the stated £48 cost of each damaged or lost parcel. ParcelLine's damage and loss rates (0.9% and 8 per 10,000) versus SwiftDrop's (0.4% and 3 per 10,000) imply about 231 extra problem parcels a month (about £11,100), far exceeding the £2,940 price saving; ParcelLine is likely the most expensive option overall.

REVIEW:
# Review: Standard Parcel Delivery Contract comparison

**Verdict: not ready to send.** The paper's own trial data contradict the recommendation. ParcelLine fails two of the four stated requirements. Once damage and loss costs are included, it is the most expensive option, not the cheapest. A decision-maker who reads Table 1 closely will see this straight away.

## Critical issues

**1. ParcelLine missed the 95% on-time threshold.**
Section 2 sets on-time delivery of at least 95%. Table 1 shows ParcelLine at **93.1%**. Section 3 says "On-time delivery was above 95% for all three carriers", and Section 7 says ParcelLine "met our service requirements". Both statements are false. Your summary repeats the claim, so it may be worth checking where it came from. On roughly 5,000 parcels per carrier, the 3-point gap to SwiftDrop is far too large to be chance.

**2. ParcelLine missed the damage threshold, and the paper never mentions it.**
The requirement is a damage rate below 0.5%. ParcelLine's rate was **0.9%**, more than double SwiftDrop's and triple Meridian's. It also lost the most parcels (8 per 10,000 against 3 and 2). The paper says damage is commercially important and costs £48 per incident, then never uses that figure.

**3. Once damage and loss are costed, ParcelLine is the most expensive.**
Using the paper's own figures for 42,000 parcels a month and £48 per damaged or lost parcel:

| Carrier | Delivery | Damage + loss | WISMO contacts (£3.20) | **All-in / month** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| SwiftDrop | £149,100 | 0.43% → £8,669 | 462 → £1,478 | **£159,247** |
| ParcelLine | £146,160 | 0.98% → £19,757 | 252 → £806 | **£166,723** |
| Meridian | £152,460 | 0.32% → £6,451 | 420 → £1,344 | **£160,255** |

- ParcelLine costs about **£7,500 a month (≈ £90,000 a year) more than SwiftDrop**, and about £6,500 a month more than Meridian.
- This holds even if ParcelLine gets full credit for the reduction in customer contacts.
- The cost of extra one-star reviews is not included, so the real gap is likely wider.

**4. The customer-contact advantage is confounded.**
Section 5 says that from 1 May, *only ParcelLine parcels* carried the new proactive delivery-day text. That covers half the trial. The lower contact rate therefore can't be put down to ParcelLine's app: the text message is an equally plausible cause, and it is ours, so we would get the benefit with any carrier. "Clearly reduces customer contacts" should be removed, or the analysis limited to April data only.

## Other issues

- **"Saving up to £76,000 a year against the alternatives" (Section 7)** is misleading even on delivery price alone. £76k is the saving against Meridian only. Against the nearest competitor, SwiftDrop, it is about £35k. (The arithmetic in Section 4 is otherwise correct: £3.55 / £3.48 / £3.63 per parcel, £2,940 and £6,300 a month.)
- **The "£670 a month" contact saving** is measured against SwiftDrop only. Against Meridian it is about £540.
- **Peak-season risk is understated.** The trial ran in April and May. The contract starts in October and covers peak season straight away. ParcelLine is the only carrier without references for peak volumes at our size, and its references are mainly for lighter parcels. That matters because 30% of our parcels are 2–10 kg lamps, mirrors and furniture, which are the items most likely to be damaged. Section 6 notes this but the recommendation ignores it.
- **Loss figures rest on small counts.** 8 vs 3 per 10,000 on about 5,000 parcels is roughly 4 vs 1–2 parcels, so treat loss as directional only. The damage and on-time differences are large enough to rely on.
- **The 12-month term** is presented as flexibility. It is equally available from SwiftDrop, so it doesn't distinguish ParcelLine.
- **Timing:** the paper is dated June 2026 for an award from 1 October 2026, and it is now mid-November. If this is going to decision-makers now, the dates and context need updating, or the paper should say what has happened since.

## What the data actually support

- **SwiftDrop** meets every requirement, has the lowest all-in cost, offers a 12-month term and has peak-season references. On this evidence it is the natural recommendation.
- **Meridian** has the best service figures and is within about £1,000 a month of SwiftDrop all-in. The 24-month commitment is its main drawback.
- **ParcelLine** could only be justified with new evidence: a credible plan to bring damage and on-time rates within requirements, backed by contractual service credits that cover the £48-per-incident cost.

## Suggested fixes before circulating

1. Correct the false statements in Sections 3 and 7 about ParcelLine meeting requirements.
2. Add damage and loss costs (and optionally contact costs) to the cost comparison, using an all-in table like the one above.
3. Remove or qualify the claim that the tracking app causes fewer contacts, and note that the delivery-day text was confined to ParcelLine.
4. Reconsider the recommendation. It currently follows from headline price alone, not from the evidence in the paper.
5. If you have it, add a breakdown of damage by weight band. This would show whether a split award (for example, light parcels to one carrier and heavy to another) is worth considering.

I can redraft Sections 4, 5 and 7 on this basis if that would help.
